ct-w1-q8.question: The cards in Pile 1 have Values in this order: 2, 3, 4. What will be the value of `p` after the pseudocode below runs?

ct-w1-q9.question: Pile 1 has 5 cards and the pseudocode below runs. When the loop ends, how many cards will Pile 1 and Pile 2 have?

ct-w1-q10.question: The cards' Values are in this order: 7, 3, 9, 4. What will be the value of `second` after the loop?

ct-w1-q13.question: The cards' Values are in this order: 4, 2, 5, 3. What will be the value of `y` after the pseudocode?

ct-w1-q14.question: The 5 cards of a pile have an average of 20. One card (Value 32) was taken out and 2 new cards were put in: 14 and x. Now the 6 cards of the pile have an average of 18. What is the value of x?

ct-w1-q15.question: A student claims this pseudocode finds the average of the cards. The cards' Values are in this order: 8, 3, 10, 5. What will be the value of `avg` after the loop?

ct-w2-q1.question: Students dataset: (Anu, Delhi, 72), (Bittu, Patna, 55), (Chinu, Delhi, 48), (Disha, Patna, 90), (Eshan, Ranchi, 60). The fields are Name, City, Marks. How many students have Marks >= 60?

ct-w2-q2.question: Same dataset: (Anu, Delhi, 72), (Bittu, Patna, 55), (Chinu, Delhi, 48), (Disha, Patna, 90), (Eshan, Ranchi, 60). For how many students is the condition `X.City == "Delhi" or X.Marks > 80` True?

ct-w2-q3.question: Dataset: (Anu, Delhi, 72), (Bittu, Patna, 55), (Chinu, Delhi, 48), (Disha, Patna, 90), (Eshan, Ranchi, 60). What will be the value of `s` after the pseudocode?

ct-w2-q4.question: Which condition is `not (X.Marks < 60)` equivalent to?
ct-w2-q4.explanation: 'Not less than 60' means 60 or more, i.e. `>= 60`. A common mistake is writing `> 60` — but at X.Marks = 60, `not (60 < 60)` = `not False` = True, so 60 is included as well.

ct-w2-q5.question: The dataset has 5 students, of whom 2 are from Patna. What will `count` be after this pseudocode?

ct-w2-q6.question: Dataset: (Anu, Delhi, 72), (Bittu, Patna, 55), (Chinu, Delhi, 48), (Disha, Patna, 90), (Eshan, Ranchi, 60). Assume Python-like precedence (`and` is evaluated first, then `or`). For how many students is the condition below True?

ct-w2-q7.question: How will you write the condition 'Price is at least 200 and at most 500' in pseudocode?
ct-w2-q7.explanation: 'At least 200' = `>= 200` and 'at most 500' = `<= 500`, and both must be true together, so AND. The option with `>` and `<` leaves out the boundary values 200 and 500. The OR option is True for every price, and the last option is never True.

ct-w2-q8.question: Cricket dataset (Name, Role, Runs): (Arjun, Batter, 45), (Bhanu, Bowler, 12), (Chetan, AllRounder, 38), (Dhruv, Bowler, 25), (Farhan, Bowler, 30). For how many players is the condition `X.Role == "Bowler" and X.Runs > 20` True?

ct-w2-q9.question: Which of these is a condition (Boolean expression), whose result is True or False?

ct-w2-q10.question: Canteen dataset (Item, Type, Price): (Samosa, Veg, 20), (Roll, NonVeg, 60), (Paneer, Veg, 130), (Biryani, NonVeg, 150), (Dosa, Veg, 90), (Kebab, NonVeg, 120). What is the average Price of the Veg items?

ct-w2-q11.question: Canteen dataset (Item, Type, Price): (Samosa, Veg, 20), (Roll, NonVeg, 60), (Paneer, Veg, 130), (Biryani, NonVeg, 150), (Dosa, Veg, 90), (Kebab, NonVeg, 120). For how many items is the condition `not (X.Type == "Veg" and X.Price < 100)` True?

ct-w2-q12.question: Canteen dataset (Item, Type, Price): (Samosa, Veg, 20), (Roll, NonVeg, 60), (Paneer, Veg, 130), (Biryani, NonVeg, 150), (Dosa, Veg, 90), (Kebab, NonVeg, 120). The cards are in Pile 1 in this order. What will `a` and `b` be after the pseudocode?

ct-w2-q13.question: Canteen dataset (Item, Type, Price): (Samosa, Veg, 20), (Roll, NonVeg, 60), (Paneer, Veg, 130), (Biryani, NonVeg, 150), (Dosa, Veg, 90), (Kebab, NonVeg, 120). ct-w2-q14.question: In a class of 100 students: 40 students are from Delhi, 30 students have Marks > 80, and 12 students are from Delhi and also have Marks > 80. For how many students is the condition `X.City == "Delhi" or X.Marks > 80` True?

ct-w2-q15.question: Canteen dataset (Item, Type, Price): (Samosa, Veg, 20), (Roll, NonVeg, 60), (Paneer, Veg, 130), (Biryani, NonVeg, 150), (Dosa, Veg, 90), (Kebab, NonVeg, 120). The cards are in Pile 1 in this order. What will be the value of `up` after the pseudocode?

ct-w3-q1.question: What datatype is the result of the condition `X.Price > 100`?
ct-w3-q1.explanation: A comparison always results in True or False, so it's Boolean. X.Price itself may be an Integer, but the whole expression `X.Price > 100` gives a Boolean — this is the common confusion.

ct-w3-q2.question: For which of these fields is Integer the most suitable datatype?
options: Quantity of items in an order
ct-w3-q2.explanation: Adding, subtracting, averaging quantities — all of it is meaningful, so Integer. PIN codes and mobile numbers are made of digits, but arithmetic on them has no meaning, so it's better to treat them like Strings.

ct-w3-q3.question: Here `+` joins (concatenates) two Strings. What will be the value of `c`?
ct-w3-q3.explanation: a and b are both in quotes, i.e. Strings. String + String = join the two, keeping the same order: "12" followed by "3" → "123". 15 would come if both were Integers; a space doesn't appear in between on its own.

ct-w3-q4.question: A subtype is defined for the Marks field: an Integer from 0 to 100 (both 0 and 100 included). Which value is valid in this subtype?
ct-w3-q4.explanation: 100 is an Integer and within the range (the boundary is included). 101 and -5 are outside the range, and 72.5 isn't even an Integer — both conditions of the subtype (Integer + range) must be satisfied.

ct-w3-q5.question: A record has the fields: RollNo (e.g. 1045), Name (String), Maths (Integer marks 0–100). Which operation is meaningful?
options: Finding the average of all RollNos
Finding the average of all students' Maths marks

ct-w3-q6.question: What is the value and datatype of `s` after the pseudocode?

ct-w3-q7.question: What is the value of `length("New Delhi")`?
ct-w3-q7.explanation: A String's length is the number of characters in it, and a space is a character too: N-e-w (3) + space (1) + D-e-l-h-i (5) = 9. 8 comes if you don't count the space; 2 is the number of words, not characters.

ct-w3-q8.question: Which of these values is a Boolean?
ct-w3-q8.explanation: A Boolean has only two values, True and False, and they are written without quotes. `"True"` is in quotes, so it is a String (this is the common mistake). `'T'` is a Character and `1` is an Integer.

ct-w3-q9.question: Which operation is the most meaningful on two Boolean values (like `X.Paid` and `X.Delivered`)?
ct-w3-q9.explanation: Boolean values behave like conditions, so they are combined with `and` / `or` (and `not`), e.g. `X.Paid and X.Delivered`. `+` and average are operations on numbers (Integer), and length belongs to a String — not to a Boolean.

ct-w3-q10.question: Here `+` joins (concatenates) Strings. What will be the value of `n` after the pseudocode?
ct-w3-q10.explanation: c = "Data" + " " + "Sci" = "Data Sci". Length: 4 (Data) + 1 (space) + 3 (Sci) = 8. 7 comes if you forget the space in the middle — it is a String that was joined too. 2 is the number of Strings and 3 is only b's length.

ct-w3-q11.question: A student record has the fields: Name (String), Gender (Character, 'M' or 'F'), Marks (Integer 0–100), Passed (Boolean). Which pseudocode line is correct with respect to datatypes?

The first compares a Boolean with the String "True" (a Boolean has no quotes). The second adds a String to a numeric total, and the fourth puts the String "85" into an Integer field.

ct-w3-q12.question: On each card the `Letter` field is a Character, and `+` joins Strings/Characters. In which order should the cards be placed so that `same` is True after the loop?
ct-w3-q12.explanation: w joins the letters in the same order, while r puts each new letter in front — so r is always w reversed. same is True only when the word stays the same when reversed. ct-w3-q13.question: Pile 1 has 3 cards. Here `+` joins two Strings. What will be the value of `count` after the loop?
ct-w3-q13.explanation: count is the String "0" from the start, and on each card the String "1" is joined: "0" → "01" → "011" → "0111". `+` on quoted values is joining (concatenation), not counting. 3 would come if `count = 0` and `count + 1` were Integers; "3" is wrong too, because no number is calculated here at all. 4 is the length of the final String.

ct-w3-q14.question: Subtype Percent = an Integer from 0 to 100 (both included). a and b are both of type Percent. Which result stays inside the Percent subtype for every possible a, b?
options: Whichever of a and b is bigger
ct-w3-q14.explanation: The bigger one is itself either a or b, so it is always an Integer from 0–100. `a + b`: 70 + 50 = 120, outside the range. `a - b`: 30 - 50 = -20. `(a + b) / 2` does stay in the range, but for 71 and 80 it gives 75.5, which is not an Integer — the subtype needs both conditions (Integer + range).

ct-w3-q15.question: The `Paid` field (Boolean) of the bill cards is in this order: True, False, True, True. What will `p` and `q` be after the loop?
ct-w3-q15.explanation: p: True and True = True → True and False = False → False and True = False → False and True = False. Once it is False, `and` never lets it become True again, so p tells whether all the bills are paid. q is overwritten on every card, and the last card is True → q = True. 'p = True' would come if p also looked only at the last card; 'q = False' if you thought q also gets stuck at False.

ct-w4-q1.question: Which shape is used in a flowchart to check a condition?
ct-w4-q1.explanation: The diamond is the decision box — the condition is written in it and two paths (Yes/No) come out of it. The rectangle is for processes, the oval for Start/End and the parallelogram for input/output.

ct-w4-q2.question: In a flowchart, which shape is used for an output step like 'Print total'?
ct-w4-q2.explanation: Input and output are both shown in a parallelogram. The diamond is only for conditions and the oval only for Start/End; an arrow only shows the direction of flow, not a step.

ct-w4-q3.question: What will be the output of this flowchart?
ct-w4-q3.explanation: Trace: x = 2 → y = 1, x = 6. x = 6 → y = 2, x = 18. x = 18 < 20 → y = 3, x = 54. Now 54 < 20 is No → Output y = 3. The 2 trap comes if you mistakenly take 18 < 20 as No; 54 is the value of x, not y.

ct-w4-q4.question: In this flowchart, how many times in total is the decision box (`n > 0 ?`) evaluated?
ct-w4-q4.explanation: n = 5 (Yes), n = 3 (Yes), n = 1 (Yes), n = -1 (No). Three Yes and one No → 4 checks in total. The most common mistake is saying 3 — the last check, the one that gives No, is counted too. (9 is the final value of s.)

ct-w4-q5.question: What is true about this flowchart?
options: The loop runs 5 times and stops
The loop doesn't run even once
The loop never stops, because i is never equal to 10
ct-w4-q5.explanation: The values of i are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13… — all odd, so 10 never comes. That's why `i != 10` stays True forever and the loop is infinite. The 5-times option would be right if the condition were `i < 10`.

ct-w4-q6.question: The cards in the pile have values: 4, 9, 12, 15, 7. `%` means remainder (e.g. `12 % 3 = 0`). What will a and b be at the End of the flowchart?
ct-w4-q6.explanation: 4: not divisible by 3, even → b = 1. 9: divisible by 3 → a = 1. 12: divisible by 3 → a = 2 (it never even reaches D3). 15 → a = 3. 7: nothing. Answer a = 3, b = 1. The b = 2 trap comes if you also count 12 as even — but D3 is only on D2's No path.

ct-w4-q7.question: How many paths (exits) come out of a decision box (diamond) in a flowchart?
ct-w4-q7.explanation: A decision box checks a condition whose result is True or False, so two paths come out: Yes and No. A box with only one arrow out is a process box (rectangle), not a decision. If you need more choices, several diamonds are placed one after another.

ct-w4-q8.question: What will be the output of this flowchart?
ct-w4-q8.explanation: Is 7 > 12? No, so the No path: m = b = 12, then Output m → 12. This flowchart gives the bigger of the two numbers. 7 comes if you take the Yes path, 19 is the sum and 5 the difference.

ct-w4-q9.question: How do you recognise a loop in a flowchart?
options: When an arrow goes back to an earlier decision box
When the flowchart has two ovals
When a parallelogram appears in the flowchart
When a condition is written in a rectangle
ct-w4-q9.explanation: A loop is formed when an arrow comes back to an earlier decision box — the same steps run again until the other path of the decision is taken. The two ovals are just Start and End, a parallelogram is input/output, and a condition is always written in a diamond, never in a rectangle.

ct-w4-q10.question: What will be the output of this flowchart?
ct-w4-q10.explanation: Trace: n = 1 → s = 1, n = 3. n = 3 → s = 4, n = 5. n = 5 → s = 9, n = 7. n = 7 <= 7 Yes → s = 16, n = 9. 9 <= 7 No → Output 16. 9 comes if you skip the n = 7 round (`<=` includes 7). 28 = the sum of all numbers from 1 to 7, and 25 also adds 9.

ct-w4-q11.question: What will be the output at the End of this flowchart?
ct-w4-q11.explanation: n: 50 → 42 → 34 → 26 → 18 → 10 → 2, and c goes up each time → c = 6. Now 2 >= 8 is No, so Output c = 6, n = 2. This is like dividing 50 by 8: quotient 6, remainder 2. 'c = 5, n = 10' is the mistake of stopping one round early (10 >= 8 is still Yes), and 'c = 7, n = -6' is one round too many.

ct-w4-q12.question: The pile has ticket cards (Age, Day): (8, Sunday), (65, Sunday), (30, Sunday), (60, Monday), (25, Friday). What will be the flowchart's output (total)?
ct-w4-q12.explanation: 8: Age < 12 → 50. 65: >= 60 → 60. 30: neither a child nor a senior, Sunday → 150. 60: `>= 60` includes 60 → 60. 25: Friday → 100. Total = 50 + 60 + 150 + 60 + 100 = 420. 460 comes if you don't treat the 60-year-old as a senior (charging 100). 520 comes if you charge the child the Sunday 150 — but only those who get No at both D2 and D3 reach D4. 370 forgets the Sunday 150.

ct-w4-q13.question: `%` means remainder. The output of this flowchart was 4. Which of these was the input N?
ct-w4-q13.explanation: Trace every option. 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: 4 steps, output 4. 12 → 6 → 3 → 4 → 2 → 1: 5 steps (3 is odd, so +1 happens). 10 → 5 → 6 → 3 → 4 → 2 → 1: 6 steps. 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: 3 steps. Only N = 16 gives 4. The trap is 8: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 has 4 numbers in it, and D1 is also checked 4 times (3 Yes + the final No), so 4 is easy to say. ct-w12-q12.question: When `c(4)` is called once, how many times in total is the function `c` called (including the first call)?
ct-w12-q12.explanation: Let C(n) be the total number of calls made when c(n) runs. C(0) = C(1) = 1 (just itself). C(2) = 1 + C(1) + C(0) = 3. C(3) = 1 + C(2) + C(1) = 5. C(4) = 1 + C(3) + C(2) = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9. 3 is the return value of c(4) (0, 1, 1, 2, 3), not the number of calls. 16 = 2 to the power 4 — it assumes every call makes 2 full calls, but c(1) and c(0) stop at the base case.

ct-w12-q13.question: What will be the output of this Python code (each `print` on its own line; here the lines are written with commas)?
ct-w12-q13.explanation: show(2): first print 2, then call show(1). show(1): print 1, then show(0) — which returns immediately — then the second print 1. Now back in show(2), its second print 2. Output: 2, 1, 1, 2. The first print runs on the way down and the second during unwinding (on the way back) — so 1 appears twice in the middle and 2 on the outside. '2, 1' comes if you think the line after the recursive call never runs.
